claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations and heterogeneous microstructural features.
In situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction during micro-scale tensile testing can directly track evolving phase distributions in HfNbTiVAl10.
In situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction can directly track lattice strains in the tested material.
High-resolution X-ray tomography during loading can directly track void and crack initiation and propagation.
The measured phase, lattice-strain, and damage observables can be used to calibrate a continuum damage mechanics model.
Linking measured microstructural evolution to macroscopic stress-strain responses enables prediction of Young's modulus.
Linking measured microstructural evolution to macroscopic stress-strain responses enables prediction of yield strength.
A continuum damage mechanics model calibrated primarily from the proposed in situ observations can predict fracture toughness.
The proposed experimentally calibrated model bypasses the high computational overhead of CALPHAD, first-principles, and machine-learning approaches.
The approach will improve predictive accuracy by approximately 25–30% relative to the prior computational methods.
The approach will reduce model-calibration and simulation time by about 50% relative to the prior computational methods.
Existing high-fidelity simulations and machine-learning models are computationally demanding.
Existing simulation and machine-learning methods lack robust fracture-toughness prediction for this application.
The method is reliable only near the calibrated strain rate.
The method is reliable only near ambient temperature.
The method's reliability depends on maintaining the calibrated synchrotron imaging conditions.
Insufficient temporal or spatial resolution may make the proposed approach ineffective.
Experimental noise, beam quality, and specimen preparation can affect predictive accuracy.
